title: The blue note as a passing tone

review.reviewedBy: Claude, the AI that wrote it

inspiration.note: Burrell is a model of blues playing inside jazz, and Midnight Blue is the classic example: blues-scale phrases with space around them, slides for a vocal sound, and question-and-answer phrasing. This lick borrows the blue note as a passing tone, a slide into the target and a short answer phrase.

analysis.summary: A blues-scale line falls from the 3rd of {{chord 1}} to its 4th, with the flat 5th, the blue note, passing between the 5th and the 4th. The line turns back up and slides a half step from the 5th of {{chord 1}} into the 3rd of {{chord 2}}, right on the chord change. After a breath, a short answer comes back to the same 3rd.

points.text: The line starts by walking down {{chord 1}}: 3rd, root, 7th and 5th ({{note 1.2}} to {{note 1.5}}). Over {{chord 2}} it lands on the 3rd ({{note 2.1}}), touches the 5th in the answer ({{note 2.4}}) and ends on the 3rd again ({{note 3.1}}).

The 4th of a minor chord, also called its 11th, is a soft, bluesy colour: {{note 1.7}} over {{chord 1}} and {{note 2.3}} over {{chord 2}}. Both belong to the minor pentatonic scale of {{key}}, so they blend in.

{{note 1.6}} is the blue note, the flat 5th of {{chord 1}}. It is not in the chord, but it is safe because it only passes: it splits the whole step between the 5th and the 4th into two half steps and keeps moving. {{note 1.8}} then slides up a half step into the target, and in the answer {{note 2.5}} steps down a whole step onto it.

The line starts on the 'and' of 1 and runs in even eighth notes. The blue note falls on an offbeat, the 'and' of 3, so it passes lightly. The slide arrives exactly on beat 1 of {{chord 2}}; after a breath, the answer starts on the 'and' of 3 and lands on beat 1 again.

{{note 2.1}} is the 3rd of {{chord 2}}, the note that tells the ear the chord has changed. It is only a half step above the 5th of {{chord 1}}, so the slide joins the two chords like a voice bending into the note.

whyItWorks: A blue note sounds best on the move. The flat 5th lasts half a beat, squeezed between the 5th and the 4th, so the ear hears a bluesy smear, not a wrong note. The slide then turns the chord change into one vocal gesture, and ending the answer on the same 3rd makes it sound like it agrees with the question.
fingeringNote: Second minor-pentatonic box (tenth position in the lesson's original key): index finger on the lowest fret of the shape, one finger per fret, with the middle finger on the blue note. At the end of bar 1 the ring finger slides up one fret into the landing note. The hand moves up with it, so play the answer from there with the index and ring fingers.
practiceTask: Play the lick over bars 2 to 4 of the weekly standard. Start with bar 1 alone at a slow tempo and listen to the blue note pass, then add the slide and the answer. Finally try the variation, where the blue note passes on the way up.

variation.description: The blue note now passes on the way up. The arpeggio falls to the 3rd of {{chord 1}}, then the line climbs 4th, flat 5th and 5th ({{note 1.6}}, {{note 1.7}}, {{note 1.8}}) and keeps rising into the slide. {{note 1.7}} is still a passing tone between the 5th and the 4th, just in the other direction; it now falls on beat 4 instead of an offbeat, so keep it light and keep moving.
